query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin hafnium‐rich interlayer within a high-entropy-alloy bond coat will promote the formation of a graded Hf–Zr transition at the coating–substrate interface and thereby improve adhesion, slow oxygen ingress, and reduce oxide scale spallation under high-temperature corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard high-entropy-alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi‑based or a refractory HEA) bond coat applied on a substrate that contains elements (such as zirconium) capable of interacting with hafnium, without any additional reactive element doping.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a calibrated, thin hafnium-rich interlayer into the fabrication process of the bond coat (for example, by co-doping or depositing a Hf-rich precursor layer) so that during high-temperature exposure, diffusion occurs at the interface.
generation.conditions: The coating is used in high-temperature oxidation environments (approximately 900 °C) and in the presence of corrosive molten salts (e.g., mixtures of Na2SO4 and NaCl), as typically found in thermal barrier coating systems for gas turbines or steam pipelines.
generation.structural_mediator: The interdiffusion between the hafnium in the interlayer and the zirconium (or similar reactive elements) present in the substrate leads to the in situ formation of a graded Hf–Zr alloy layer. This gradient acts as a robust mediator enhancing the metallurgical bond and serving as a barrier to oxygen and corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, hafnium diffuses into the adjacent substrate where it reacts with readily mobile elements (e.g., Zr) to form an intermetallic gradient. This graded layer improves adhesion by reducing the interface energy and retards oxidation by lowering oxygen diffusion, thus mitigating scale spallation and prolonging the service life of the protective coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat with the hafnium-rich interlayer should exhibit significantly reduced oxide scale spallation, improved adhesion at the coating–substrate interface, and overall enhanced durability and reliability compared to standard, untreated HEA bond coats.
generation.baseline: Standard high-entropy-alloy bond coats produced without any added reactive (hafnium-rich) interlayer.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to persist under high-temperature (∼900 °C) conditions and oxidizing environments with molten salt exposure, but may be limited if processing parameters do not allow sufficient interdiffusion to form a robust graded interlayer.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal hafnium content and interlayer thickness need systematic optimization, and long-term cyclic thermal effects and mechanical fatigue on the gradient layer remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set with a standard HEA bond coat on a Zr-containing substrate and a second set incorporating a thin hafnium-rich interlayer intended to form a graded Hf–Zr interface. Expose both groups to high-temperature (∼900 °C) conditions in a molten salt (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) environment for a fixed duration.
measurements: Quantify the oxide spallation area on the coating surface via image analysis after exposure
Perform pull-off adhesion tests to measure bond strength at the interface
Measure weight gain (oxidation kinetics) during exposure
Use cross-sectional EDS and XRD analyses to confirm the formation and composition of the graded Hf–Zr interlayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the hafnium-rich interlayer do not show statistically significant improvements in adhesion (higher pull-off strength), reduced oxide spallation (lower spallation area), and/or enhanced oxidation resistance (lower weight gain) relative to the standard bond coats, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,]. Research about the effect of alloying elements on the performance of HEAs has predominantly concentrated on the mechanical properties while the literature indicates that conventional and high-entropy alloys and Y and Hf co-doping can effectively enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance of alloys [,,].
